sections.heading: Product information lives in too many places
paragraphs: Specifications sit in PLM, bills of materials in ERP, supplier declarations in email and test reports on a shared drive. A Digital Product Passport needs all of it, linked to one product and kept up to date.

Under the EU Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) and the Battery Regulation, more and more product groups need a passport. Teams that start collecting data the week before a deadline end up with gaps they cannot close in time.

sections.heading: From product identity to passport workflow
sections.intro: One workspace, connected data. Every passport is built from the same four building blocks.

items.title: 01 · Build a product record
items.text: Product identity, category, model and country of manufacture, captured once and reused in every passport.

items.title: 02 · Map the composition
items.text: Bills of materials, component records and a reusable material library with origin and recycled-content details.

items.title: 03 · Keep evidence in context
items.text: Supplier, environmental and other supporting information, attached to the product it belongs to.

items.title: 04 · Review readiness
items.text: See data gaps at a glance, then move the passport through validation, publication and its lifecycle.

sections.heading: Make progress one product at a time
sections.intro: You do not need a perfect data landscape to begin. Start with one product and extend from there.

items.title: Bring the record together
items.text: Create the product, import what you already have and see immediately which information is missing.

items.title: Connect the detail
items.text: Link materials, components and suppliers, and attach the declarations and test reports that support them.

items.title: Review and publish
items.text: Check readiness, close the gaps and publish a machine-readable passport behind a QR code.

items.title: Submit and track
items.text: Submit eligible passports to the EU registry, follow their processing and keep the outcomes as evidence.

sections.heading: Which passports are coming, and when
rows: EV, LMT and industrial batteries above 2 kWh
sections.after: ESPR dates follow the Commission's working plan 2025–2030 and are indicative. Obligations usually apply about 18 months after a delegated act is adopted.

sections.heading: Built around the complexity of physical products

items.title: Manufacturing
items.text: Many variants, many suppliers: reuse materials and evidence across product families.

items.title: Automotive and mobility
items.text: Deep supply chains and components that travel through several tiers before they reach the vehicle.

items.title: Batteries and electronics
items.text: The first mandatory passports, with detailed composition, carbon footprint and due-diligence data.

items.title: Industrial components
items.text: Long-lived products whose passport must stay accurate through repair, refurbishment and reuse.

items.text: We map where your product, material and supplier data lives today and what is missing for your product group.

items.title: Integration with ERP and PLM

items.title: Registry connection support

items.q: What is a Digital Product Passport?
items.a: A digital record of a product's identity, composition, origin and sustainability information, reachable through a data carrier such as a QR code. The EU requires passports for batteries from February 2027 and, step by step, for further product groups under the ESPR.

items.q: Is a registered passport a compliance certificate?
items.a: No. Registration in the EU registry is not a compliance certification, and DPPSpace is not an EU institution or certification body. DPPSpace helps you prepare, publish and register the data. Responsibility for the content stays with the economic operator.

items.q: Do we need all our data before we start?
items.a: No. Start with one product, see what is missing and fill the gaps step by step. The readiness view shows exactly which information is still open.

items.q: Who can see the data in a passport?
items.a: Each regulation defines which information is public and which is reserved for authorities or other parties with a legitimate interest. DPPSpace keeps your working data in your workspace and publishes only what the passport should show.
